newsitem.title: UK: Next British government urged to slash deficit.
newsitem.headline: Next British government urged to slash deficit.

text.p: The next British government will have to cut spending sharply or raise taxes to prevent a serious deterioration in the public finances, according to a leading economic think-tank.

In a report released on Wednesday, a day before the election, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR) said it saw no need for a widely anticipated post-election increase in interest rates.

But although the next government, which opinion polls suggest will be formed by the opposition Labour party, would take over an economy in generally good shape, urgent action was needed to curb the budget deficit.
"The new government will inherit an unhealthy fiscal position, with public sector borrowing higher than would normally be expected at this stage of the economic cycle," the institute said.
The report was co-authored by Martin Weale, director of the NIESR and a member of Conservative Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's panel of economic advisers, known as the "wise people."

The NIESR said the public sector's balance sheet had deteriorated rapidly over the last five years of Conservative rule, as the government increased borrowing and sold off assets, largely by privatising former state-owned companies.
It blamed the worsening public finances mainly on "laxity in public expenditure at the beginning of the decade, which has not subsequently been fully corrected."
"The deterioration in the balance sheet cannot continue at this rate," it said. "The government would eventually face a situation in which it could not raise the taxes needed to service its debts."

The report, nevertheless, concluded that Britain's budget deficit was likely to fall to 1.3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1998/99 from 3.1 percent in 1996/97, allowing the country to meet the deficit ratio laid down in the Maastricht Treaty for joining a single European currency.
But it said a tightening of fiscal policy of about 2.5 percent of GDP -- 15 billion to 20 billion pounds -- was needed.

The Labour party, anxious to shake off its past image as a party of high taxation, has ruled out increasing income tax rates and pledged to live within tough public spending limits laid down by the Conservatives for the next two years.

The NIESR said the best time to tighten fiscal policy was at the start of a new parliament, but it thought large-scale tax increases unlikely in the near future and the next government was more likely to curb spending instead.

The NIESR expects a Labour government to stick to tough spending plans, while boosting revenue by increasing taxes on dividends and freezing personal tax allowances at current levels for the next three years.

The institute gave an otherwise favourable assessment of Britain's economic prospects, saying there was little evidence of inflationary pressures building up as the strength of the pound was dampening imported inflation.

It assumed interest rates would be raised to around 6.5 percent by the middle of the year from the present 6.0 percent in deference to the Bank of England's argument that there is a risk of the economy overheating.
But this would be reversed by the beginning of 1998, by which time it would have become clear that higher rates were unnecessary.
